source.author: Geoffrey Khan
source.edition: The Tiberian Pronunciation Tradition of Biblical Hebrew I, section I.1.1, printed pp. 135-149
source.access: Indexed Cambridge-hosted PDF inspected by page/lines (local PDF requests blocked). Named manuscript readings below are via Khan; no manuscript image independently inspected.

cases.witness: Khan's reconstruction of standard Tiberian Hebrew
cases.finding: Reconstructs a glottal stop in medial onset after silent shewa or after a vowel, and in medial coda respectively. These are phonetic transcriptions, not preserved audio.

cases.witness: Hidāyat al-Qāriʾ, long version II.L.1.3.2 in Khan vol. II; Masora magna, BL Harley 1528 (fourteenth-century Spain), as explicitly cited via Ginsburg 1880 section 5 in Khan n.2
cases.finding: The received list singles out four marked medial occurrences. A mark records a reading instruction; length vs consonantal articulation is a separate interpretive issue.

cases.witness: Leningrad Codex L versus Aleppo Codex A as collated by Khan
cases.finding: L has two additional marked examples beside the canonical four. Distinguish manuscript occurrence from canonical list membership.

cases.witness: Cambridge T-S NS 248.2, as cited by Khan via Arrant 2020, compared with L [BHS]
cases.finding: Certain word-final alefs carry a dot even though Khan reconstructs them as non-consonantal. This witness contradicts universal decoding of the dot as an obligatory glottal closure.

exposure: All named loci are exposed scholarly-baseline examples. No prediction tested.
transfer: These dated traditions constrain medieval readings. The older Arad and Elephantine editions supply graphemic identifications but lack this medieval witness evidence. No bridge yet justifies projecting the Tiberian context rules, gemination or pitch onto them. A lack of measured pitch is not evidence against a specific historical pitch.
